newsitem.title: USA: NHL-KONSTANTINOV IN COMA, SHOWING POSITIVE SIGNS.
newsitem.headline: NHL-KONSTANTINOV IN COMA, SHOWING POSITIVE SIGNS.

text.p: Detroit Red Wings star defenceman Vladimir Konstantinov remained in a coma on Sunday with head injuries sustained in a car accident, but doctors said he is showing subtle signs of facial expression in response to music and voices.

Konstantinov, Red Wings teammate Slava Fetisov and a member of the team's training staff were injured on Friday night when the limousine they were riding in struck a tree in suburban Detroit on the way home from a team golf outing.
The crash ended six days of celebration after Konstantinov and his teammates won the Red Wings' first NHL Stanley Cup championship in 42 years on June 7.

Konstantinov, 30, a member of Detroit's vaunted "Russian Five", and the team's 43-year-old Russian masseur, Sergei Mnatsakanov, both remained in critical condition and were breathing with the help of a ventilator, said Dr. James Robbins of William Beaumont Hospital in Royal Oak.
"There has been no sign of deterioration in their condition," Robbins told reporters on Sunday. "They're being treated aggressively for any subtle changes in intracranial pressure."

Robbins said Red Wings team members have been playing tapes of Russian music for the two, and were also playing "We Are The Champions" by the rock group Queen -- a song Konstantinov frequently listened to in the past week.
Konstantinov has moved extremities, made subtle facial expressions and "seems to respond to the voices of his teammates and his family and these are extremely encouraging signs," Robbins said.
He added that doctors have seen patients with worse head injuries make full recoveries.
Konstantinov, born in Murmansk, Russia, as the son of a fisherman, has a wife, Irina, and a young daughter, Anastasia.
The Red Wings' grand old man, 39-year-old defenceman Fetisov, was upgraded from fair to good condition with chest contusions and a bruised lung. Robbins said he may be released
from the hospital in the next day or two.
Richard Gnida, the driver of the limousine, was protected by an air bag and was listed in good condition with no serious inuries.

Robbins said doctors had not found any indication that drugs or alcohol played a role in the accident, but Michigan Secretary of State records indicate that Gnida had a long history of driving violations and that his drivers' license had been revoked since last July.

Police in Birmingham, Mich., where the crash occurred, said on Sunday that earlier reports that Gnida swerved to avoid a stalled car were not true. No other vehicles were involved, and the limousine crossed two lanes of traffic before it hit the tree in the median of Woodward Avenue, said Sgt. John Van Gordon.
"He can't remember anything prior to the accident," Van Gordon said of Gnida.
Officials of Gambino's Limousine Service, which has shuttled Red Wings players to numerous parties all week long, have said they didn't know Gnida's license was revoked.
Stunned Red Wings fans continued to hold vigils outside the hospital on Sunday and left flowers, Red Wings banners and other tokens of affection at the crash site.
"This isn't something that should happen to a team that's brought a lot of love to this town," said fan Dwight Hamlin.
